response.translation: [226] But [he says] that in those who are growing the heat is not great according to substance either, given at any rate that the bulk of the body is small, nor according to the increase of the quality, for it does not appear hotter than that of those in their prime. In the strength of its proper works, indeed, he concedes that the heat of those who are growing is superior, but [says] that this is not what is properly meant by the word. Now his passage, through which he will make these things clear, is very long. But I think that I shall do now too just as I did in the case of the one quoted above: for that one too, being extremely long, I did not write out in full, but selected only the most pertinent part of it. Let it be done, then, in the same way with this one too, and let the part of it most useful for the matter in hand be written out. "The one of my two discussions, then, has indeed reached its end, and I may now come to the remaining one; for surely [one must] remember that I set out two inquiries right at the beginning: one, whether Hippocrates was right to add 'innate', the other, whether he was right to say that the heat is greatest in those who are growing.

Now that the first inquiry [227] has been brought to completion, I may turn next to this one and attempt to examine whether it has been rightly said that the heat is greatest in those who are growing. In examining one heat against another, the things that require inquiry happen to be three, and very widely separated from one another: one, what it is for one thing to be more heat than another; a second, what it is for one thing to be hotter than another; and a third, what it is for one thing to be a stronger heat than another. If, then, someone should happen to ask us what it is for one thing to be more heat than another, we ought to give the answer analogous to the one we would give to the other man who asks what it is for one thing to be more moisture than another. For just as there, once the question is put in the first place with reference to what has been stated, it is no longer correct to answer anything else except this alone, that it exceeds in substance, being more: one would doubtless say that the amphora is more moisture than the half-amphora.
uncertain_greek: ἐνταῦθα πρῶτον τὸ ἐπερώτημα πρὸς τὸ εἰρημένον

response.translation: So too in the case of heat: if someone were to put this same question, what it is for one thing to be more heat than the other, we should not correctly [228] answer anything other than that which is more in substance, evidently because it is more in substance and extends over more place. And nothing at all will prevent the same thing from being both more heat and heat to a lesser degree, just as the thing that is more moisture in substance could also be less diffused. To this question, then, one would have answered correctly in this way; but to that other question, what it is for one thing to be hotter than another, the correct answer is that which is more intensified in respect of warming, even if it happens to be in a smaller substance. Just as to one asking what it is for one thing to be whiter than another it is correct to answer: that which is more intensified in respect of the quality white. In this respect, at any rate, even if snow happens to be present in a small bulk, one would say it is whiter than any other white thing whatsoever; just as also to one asking what it is for one thing to be moister than another it is correct to answer: that which is more diffused, as water is than honey and pitch, even if the water is observed in a very small substance while the honey and the pitch are in excess.

So too [229] to one asking about heat what it is for one thing to be hotter than another it is correct to answer: that which is most intensified in respect of warming, as for instance fire, even if it is observed in a small amount of substance, while some other heat, one that is in fact lukewarm, when compared against it happens to exist in a greater substance. To these questions, then, these are the answers; but to one who inquires what it is for one thing to be a stronger heat than another, the answer is no longer like the previous ones. For we shall answer neither that which is more intensified in respect of warming nor that which is observed in a greater substance, but that which excels in the accomplishment of its work. What I mean would be established as follows. The works of heat are, surely, many. For some things are melted by it, and it makes others set, and it transforms very many things; and, to speak of our bodies in particular, it digests the food in the stomach and the intestines, and conveys the product of its working-up into the body, and alters it into body and attaches it to our bodies, in nutrition and in growth.
uncertain_greek: οὐκ ἂν ἐπ’ ὀλίγης οὐσίας θεωρεῖται

response.translation: One heat, then, is stronger than another when it is the one that will be able to furnish [230] these things to a greater degree. And what happens to be such is not in every case the one that is either intensified in respect of quality or greater in substance. For often that which is less in substance and less in warming is the most effective for the work. For, as we said before, with respect to the performance of its proper works it is not the most intensified heat that is stronger, but the most well-proportioned; since that which has been intensified in respect of warming itself sometimes even becomes a harm to the works, and for this I have as most trustworthy and sufficient [evidence] the things I set out before, when speaking about the peculiar nature of heat.
uncertain_greek: τὸ δὲ τυγχάνον ὂν οὐχὶ πάντως

response.translation: These things being so, and the things sought in comparing one heat against another being three, as I have said before, when Hippocrates says here that those who are growing have the most innate heat, [one of three things follows]: either he uses this expression in its proper sense and has stated a falsehood, or he has used the expression badly and has also stated something false, or, in order that he may seem to have said something true, [231] he must have used the expression not well. For if he says that heat is greatest in those who are growing in the sense of according to substance, as one might also say that the moisture of the amphora is greatest, not that of the double of it, he will seem to have used the expression correctly, but it is necessary that he has stated a great falsehood. For the heat in those who are growing is not greatest in substance, since neither is the bulk of the body greater in these than in those in their prime and in the old; and the innate heat extends through the whole body.

But if, on the other hand, he says that those who are growing have more [heat] and [means] this warming as intensified, presumably hotter than the other, as if someone wishing to say that snow is whiter than some other white thing should say not that it is whiter or more white, but that the white is more than this white, then Hippocrates will seem to err on both counts, both in not using the expression well and, apart from that, in saying something false. In not using the [232] expression well he would seem to go wrong because he applied this expression, which is assigned to what is greater in substance, wishing to signify that the quality is more intensified in respect of warming. And he would seem to have stated a falsehood, because the heat in those who are growing is not most intensified in respect of quality, nor is the heat, as it should be [for his claim], hotter in this age than in some other. But he said that it is most intensified in those who are growing; and that this is in fact false, that the heat is most intensified in those who are growing, is easy for anyone to establish. For no sign existing in the body would be found in those who are growing of the heat being most intensified in respect of warming. For what is said by him in the treatise On the Nature of Man, as a proof that heat is greatest in those who are growing, is utterly foolish: namely, to declare that a human being is hotter in the first period of life, inferring this from the fact that growth is then accomplished to the greatest degree.

For, he says, the nourishment would not be carried upward by force and contrary to nature, in the direction opposite to its own [233] weight, while the body is growing, unless there were something strong compelling it. But for such a thing the sign is not that the heat is more intensified in respect of warming, but that it is stronger. And the stronger, as I said a little earlier, was not such a thing as the heat most intensified in respect of its own quality, but the one most well-proportioned to its work. Since, then, these things stand thus, if Hippocrates speaks in this sense, that those who are growing have the most innate heat, he errs on both counts, both in not having used the expression well and in having, apart from that, stated something false. But if he speaks in the sense I stated third, that heat is greatest in those who are growing as equivalent to strongest for the accomplishment of its work, which comes about from its being most well-proportioned, and not from its being either greater in substance or most intensified in warming itself, then as regards the expression he would seem [not] to have used it well, because he said the heat is greatest when he ought to have said strongest; what was said, however, would seem to have been stated correctly.

For since the processes of growth come about through the [234] innate heat, as indeed the argument will state, it is impracticable and impossible that it should not be strongest in those who are growing. And to this purpose the passage from the treatise On the Nature of Man would, in my view, have been well said: for it is necessary that a body which is growing and advancing by force should have its heat strongest. Such is Lycus's passage, drawn out at length yet explaining nothing more than what was said by me before. For if Hippocrates, measuring by the bulk of the substance, said that heat is more in those who are growing, he thinks that he is in error, since the body is clearly smaller in children. And if [he meant] what is intensified in respect of warming, here again, he says, the evident facts conflict with this too. But if [he meant] what is stronger in respect of activity, he concedes that something true is being said, but declares that he has not used the word well; for the heat of those who are growing ought to have been called not more but stronger, with reference to its activity.

[235] But, my excellent Lycus, someone might say, I think, in reply to him, defending Hippocrates on the points over which he abuses him, that these statements are not faulty. To begin with, then, the heat that is more in respect of substance is not judged simply by the bulk of the whole body, but, as Lycus himself said elsewhere, [when he said] that man has the largest brain, not taking size simply but according to the proportion of animal to animal. Just as, then, he says in this way that a small child has a larger brain than the largest elephant, attending not to the bulk of the body alone but adding to it the consideration according to proportion, so he ought to have done in the case of the hot body too, having considered what sort of thing among the bodies in us is innate, that is, primordial. For he himself knows the name, both as written in the Hippocratic books and as attached to that body which exists from the beginning in those that are generated, that is, the body from which [the living thing] has had its first generation.
